common.Num: A number, or the NAME of a parameter as a string. `48` and `"hub_d"` are both valid; the string form is what makes the model parametric, and it is resolved against the document parameter table at build time.
common.PlaneSpec: Either "XY", "XZ" or "YZ", or an explicit plane {"origin":[x,y,z], "normal":[x,y,z], "xdir":[x,y,z]} in world mm. In-plane Y is normal x xdir. FundaCAD is Z-UP. Normals: XY +Z, XZ -Y (so a positive extrude from an XZ sketch goes toward -Y), YZ +X.
common.region: A 3D point INSIDE the closed sketch area you mean, in world mm. A sketch with several closed areas (a ring, a plate with holes, two separate outlines) needs one point per area you want. Omit `regions` entirely to use the whole sketch.
common.operation:
How the new material joins what is already there (default "new"): "new" makes a separate body, "join" fuses into the target, "cut" subtracts from it, "intersect" keeps only the overlap.
Without `targets`, a join/cut/intersect acts on EVERY visible body the new shape overlaps, not just the nearest one. That is what someone dragging a face across two parts means; it is not what building a second part beside a first one means. Set `targets` whenever more than one body exists. "Overlaps" is judged by bounding boxes, and an intersect REPLACES each body it hits with the overlap, so it is not a clash check.
On extrude and sweep `operation` is REQUIRED; everywhere else it defaults to "new".
common.targets:
Optional list of body ids ["body1", ...] that a join/cut/intersect is allowed to touch. Bodies not named are left alone even where the new shape passes straight through them. Ignored when `operation` is "new". A join that names targets and reaches none of them is an error rather than a quietly-created extra body.
Body ids are handed out AT BUILD TIME, so read them back from `build` or `inspect` rather than assuming them. Once built, a body keeps its id when other features are added, removed or switched off, and a join keeps the id of the body it merges into.
common.activeWhen:
Optional on EVERY feature type: a Num. While it resolves to 0 the build leaves the feature out, exactly as if it were suppressed; any other value, or no field at all, builds it. Point it at a parameter whose expression is the condition: param_set coreOn = "solidCore == 1", then "activeWhen": "coreOn". A NaN condition is an error, never read as off.
A feature that consumes a switched-off one fails and says so, so switch its consumers off with the same parameter. A switched-off body-creating feature makes no bodies; the other bodies keep their ids, but anything that used its bodies fails.
common.name: Optional on EVERY feature type: a label for the feature, which also NAMES THE BODIES IT MAKES. A box with "name":"Slider" makes a body called Slider, and that name is what `build`, the STEP file, a separate export's file names and the app's part list show. Several new bodies from one feature are "Slider 1", "Slider 2". A join or cut keeps the name of the body it works on.
common.MateConnector:
One side of a joint: a coordinate frame, an origin, a z axis that is the mating direction, and an optional x axis for rotational reference, named one of five ways:
  {"body":"body2", "face": <Selector>}   the face centre, its outward normal is the axis
  {"body":"body2", "edge": <Selector>}   the edge midpoint, its direction is the axis
  {"body":"body2", "axis": <Selector>}   a line, for pins and slides: a round face's axis through the middle of the face, a flat face's normal through its centroid, a circle's centre and normal, or a straight edge's midpoint and direction. The line points the way its largest component is positive, so a pin and the hole it sits in give the same line
  {"datum": <datumPlane id>}   follows that datum plane (a datumAxis is not supported here)
  {"origin":[x,y,z], "zdir":[x,y,z], "xdir":[x,y,z]}   an explicit world frame
A connector on geometry is a REFERENCE, re-resolved every rebuild, so the joint tracks the part as it changes. Set `body` whenever you use `face`, `edge` or `axis`. Without `xdir` the x axis is the kernel's own pick square to z, the same on both sides of a joint whose connectors give the same line.
common.active body: Where a field says "the active body", it is the most recently CREATED body; a join re-creates the body it merges into, so that body becomes the active one. Moving, filleting or cutting a body does not make it active. Name bodies explicitly whenever more than one exists.

sketch.summary: A 2D profile on a plane. Makes no geometry by itself; extrude, revolve, sweep and loft consume it.

fields.entities: the curves, see the `sketchEntities` section of this schema
fields.planeId: optional; the id of a datumPlane feature, preferred over `plane` (a `face` wins over both)
fields.face: optional Selector; makes the sketch follow a body face
fields.at: optional [x,y,z], where a round face was picked; needed with a round `face`
fields.constraints: optional; solved by the frontend, not needed for an authored sketch
fields.patterns: optional; in-sketch patterns of entity ids (patternRect, patternCircular, hexHoles, honeycomb, boltCircle, gridHoles), written by the app
fields.name: optional label

sketch.notes: Sketch coordinates are 2D IN THE PLANE. On XY they are (x, y); on XZ they are (x, z); on YZ they are (y, z). A profile to be extruded or revolved must CLOSE, the endpoints have to meet exactly, so write the same numbers, do not round differently.

fields.sketch: the id of a sketch feature
fields.distance: Num, signed; negative goes the other way

Positive narrows the far face (the way a part pulls out of a mould), negative widens it (an undercut). Must be between -89 and 89. Absent or 0 is a straight prism

fields.hiddenBodies: optional list of body ids the boolean must not touch unless `targets` names them (written by the app)

revolve.summary: Spin a sketch profile around an axis. With `pitch` it climbs as it turns, which is how a thread is made.

fields.sketch: the id of a sketch feature
fields.axis: AxisSpec. Only "X", "Y", "Z" or a line: the build reads any other name as Z, a datumAxis id included, and `validate` reports it
fields.angle: Num, degrees. 360 is a full turn
fields.operation:
How the new material joins what is already there (default "new"): "new" makes a separate body, "join" fuses into the target, "cut" subtracts from it, "intersect" keeps only the overlap.
Without `targets`, a join/cut/intersect acts on EVERY visible body the new shape overlaps, not just the nearest one. Body ids are handed out AT BUILD TIME, so read them back from `build` or `inspect` rather than assuming them. Once built, a body keeps its id when other features are added, removed or switched off, and a join keeps the id of the body it merges into.
fields.pitch: optional Num, mm of climb per full turn. With a pitch, an `angle` over 360 means more than one turn: a 2mm pitch at 1080 degrees climbs 6mm over three turns. The SIGN is the direction of climb along the axis, and a thread that cuts nothing is usually a thread climbing away from the body: try the other sign. A field takes a number or a parameter NAME, so write -2 directly, or define a parameter whose expression is -pitch and name that. "-pitch" in the field itself is an expression and is refused.
fields.axisEdge: optional Selector naming the model edge the app keeps `axis` on. The build does not re-resolve it and always spins about `axis`, so `axis` must be that edge's line
fields.regions: optional; A 3D point INSIDE the closed sketch area you mean, in world mm. A sketch with several closed areas (a ring, a plate with holes, two separate outlines) needs one point per area you want. Omit `regions` entirely to use the whole sketch.

revolve.notes: The profile must lie entirely on ONE side of the axis and must not cross it. For a thread, draw the tooth cross-section in a plane THROUGH the axis (XZ for a Z axis), set `pitch`, and wind `angle` to 360 * number_of_turns. Without `pitch` the angle is clamped to 360.

fields.profile: optional Num, clamped to -0.99..0.95: 0 (or absent) is the circular fillet, toward -1 flattens it to a chamfer's chord, toward +1 pulls it into the corner
fields.sizeType: optional "radius" (default) or "chord": chord reads `radius` as the width across the round
fields.tangentEdges: optional bool, default true: carry the round along edges tangent to the picked ones; false stops at the picked edges

fillet.notes: A SEAM edge cannot be filleted, that is the edge where a face that wraps 360 degrees closes on itself, and the kernel needs two DIFFERENT faces to blend between. `inspect` marks those edges with "seam": true. The radius must also fit: it cannot exceed the smaller of the two faces meeting at the edge.

fields.distance2: optional Num, the second distance, read only with chamferType "twoDistance"
fields.tangentEdges: optional bool, default true, as on fillet

press-pull.summary: Push one or more faces along their own normals, or along the axis of the hole they end.

fields.distance: Num, signed: positive grows the body, negative cuts in
fields.operation: optional "join" or "cut", a label that must match the sign of `distance`. It does not change what the push does, `mode` does
fields.mode: optional "auto" (the default: move the face itself, as described in the notes), or "join", "cut", "new" or "intersect": sweep the face into a prism along its normal (along the axis with `direction` "axis") by `distance` and combine that prism with the body, or with `targets`
fields.targets: optional list of body ids the prism of a non-auto `mode` is combined with, as on extrude; default the body pushed from
fields.body: optional body id; default the active body. The selectors' own `body` is NOT read here
fields.upTo: optional Selector naming a target face to stop at, instead of using `distance`
fields.taper: optional Num, degrees. Leans a PLANAR push's walls as they travel (a moulded boss, an angled pocket); positive narrows the far end. Must be between -89 and 89. Ignored on a curved face and on an `upTo` push. Absent or 0 is a straight push
fields.direction: optional, "normal" (the default) or "axis". "axis" moves the face along the line the faces around it run along instead of along its own normal, so the cone, cap or flat floor at the end of a hole slides down the hole: negative makes the hole deeper, positive shallower, and the end keeps its shape where an offset along the normal would widen it. Every face bordering the pushed one must be a wall along that line, a cylinder parallel to it or a flat wall containing it, or the feature is refused. The line is a round wall's axis, else the face's own axis, else where two flat walls meet. `taper` is ignored with "axis"
fields.followTangent: optional bool, default true. When a cylinder, cone, sphere or torus face is resized so that faces running smoothly into it would no longer meet it (a slot end made narrower than the slot), true moves that whole closed run with it so the slot narrows as one, false refuses and names those faces. Ignored on flat faces and with a non-auto mode

press-pull.notes: A planar face moves along its normal and every face around it is carried along its own surface to meet it, so a sloped side keeps its slope (the top of a frustum narrows as it rises) and a square side stays square. Where it runs into another part of the body it merges with it; where its sides meet before it gets that far it is refused. With a `taper`, or where the faces around it cannot be carried along, it extrudes into a straight prism and booleans instead. A cylinder, cone, sphere or torus keeps its axis or centre and changes size by distance along its outward normal, so a negative distance grows a hole and shrinks a boss. The faces around it keep their own surfaces and are trimmed or extended to meet it, so growing one end of a slot gives a bigger round end with the straight walls trimmed back. Selecting every face of a slot resizes the slot as one. A size at or below zero is refused, never clamped. A freeform face that WRAPS (a full revolve, a swept tube) is thickened along its own surface; `inspect` marks those faces with "wraps": true.

shell.summary: Hollow a body to a wall thickness, optionally opening faces.

fields.faces: optional Selector(s) to remove (the openings); absent = a closed hollow of the active body

offsetFace.summary: Move faces along their normals without changing the rest.

fields.body: optional body id; default the active body. The selectors' own `body` is NOT read here
fields.followTangent: optional bool, default true. When a cylinder, cone, sphere or torus face is resized so that faces running smoothly into it would no longer meet it (a slot end made narrower than the slot), true moves that whole closed run with it so the slot narrows as one, false refuses and names those faces. Ignored on flat faces and with a non-auto mode

draft.summary: Tilt faces by an angle about an axis (mould release).

hole.summary: Drill holes into a flat face along its normal: simple, counterbore, countersink, or a heat-set insert bore.

fields.face: Selector naming the flat face to drill into. Use {"kind":"face", "by":"tracked", "point":[x,y,z], "normal":[nx,ny,nz], "body":"body1"}: ONE flat face kept by its outward normal, so the holes follow it when a parameter change moves it and keep their place on it. `point` is on the face, `normal` is the face's `normal` from `inspect`. Leave `extent` out, the build writes it in
fields.points: list of [x,y,z] hole centres in world mm, projected onto the face. On a `tracked` face they are where the holes were when its `extent` was written, and each keeps its distance from the face edges it was nearest then (or stays centred) as the face moves or grows
fields.sketch: optional sketch id whose points (else circle centres) add positions; with no `face` the sketch plane gives the direction
fields.size: "M2", "M2.5", "M3", "M4", "M5", "M6", "M8" or "M10". Fills in the diameter, the counterbore, the countersink and the insert bore when left out, but not `depth`
fields.depth: Num, for a blind hole; default twice the diameter (an insert uses its preset depth)
fields.cbDiameter: Num, counterbore diameter (ISO 4762 socket head default)
fields.csDiameter: Num, countersink diameter at the face (ISO 10642 default)
fields.leadIn: Num, insert lead-in chamfer, default 0.5; 0 for none
fields.drillPoint: optional bool, a 118 degree cone at the bottom of a blind hole
fields.flip: optional bool, drill along the face normal instead of into it
fields.tapped: optional bool, a label only, no thread is modelled

hole.notes: Sizes are M2 to M10; a heat-set insert preset exists for M2 to M5 and is always blind. A through hole reaches past the far side of the body.

thicken.summary: Give a surface (or a set of faces) a thickness.

fields.faces: optional Selector(s); absent = every face of the body
fields.targets:
Optional list of body ids ["body1", ...] that a join/cut/intersect is allowed to touch. Bodies not named are left alone even where the new shape passes straight through them. Ignored when `operation` is "new". A join that names targets and reaches none of them is an error rather than a quietly-created extra body.
Body ids are handed out AT BUILD TIME, so read them back from `build` or `inspect` rather than assuming them. Once built, a body keeps its id when other features are added, removed or switched off, and a join keeps the id of the body it merges into.
fields.body: optional body id; default the active body. The selectors' own `body` is NOT read here

deleteFace.summary: Remove faces and heal the wound (defeature: takes a blend or a boss off).

fields.body: optional body id; default the active body. The selectors' own `body` is NOT read here

cleanUp.summary: Merge faces that are pieces of one surface, drop slivers.

fields.body: optional body id; absent = every body

simplifyMesh.summary: Merge near-coplanar facets of the active (most recently created) imported mesh body.

fields.tolerance: Num, DEGREES: neighbouring facets within this angle of each other merge

texture.summary: Emboss or engrave a pattern onto faces (Texture plugin).

fields.faces: optional Selector or list; absent = every face
fields.depth: optional Num, mm, greater than 0, default 0.4
fields.scale: optional Num, mm the pattern repeats over, greater than 0, default 2
fields.imagePath: optional path of the image; required with kind "image"
fields.boundaryInset: optional Num, mm the texture fades out before a face edge, default 0

texture.notes: Usually authored in the app. The finer options (grime, smooth, seamBlend, seamBand, amplitude, slopeMin, slopeMax, targetEdge, triBudget, colorSlot) are kept when a document carries them.

teardropHole.summary: Give sideways round holes a pointed or flat roof so they print without supports (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, the inside face of each hole
fields.angle: optional Num, degrees the roof leans from the build direction, 10 to 80, default 45
fields.flatHeight: optional Num, mm above the top of the hole where a flat roof sits, default 0

teardropHole.notes: Only removes material. A hole whose axis runs along the build direction is refused.

roofBridge.summary: Square off the top half of sideways round holes so the roof is a flat bridge (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, the inside face of each hole
fields.height: optional Num, mm the bridge sits above the top of the hole, default 0

counterboreBridge.summary: Cut the first layers above a counterbore floor into a slot then a square, so its ceiling bridges cleanly (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, the flat floor of each counterbore
fields.layers: optional whole Num, 1 to 3, default 2 (3 adds an octagon layer)
fields.angle: optional Num, degrees the slot turns about the bore, default 0

sacrificialLayer.summary: Close a round hole with a thin membrane to drill out after printing (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, a hole's inside face or the flat face it opens onto
fields.depth: optional Num, mm into the hole from its opening, default 0
fields.side: optional "bottom" (default) or "top", which opening a picked hole face closes

threadRibs.summary: Turn a plain round hole into a self-tapping screw hole: thin axial ribs protrude inward for the screw to cut its own thread into (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, the inside face of each hole
fields.coreDiameter: optional Num, mm, the tap/core diameter the ribs leave clear; 0 or absent defaults to 80% of the hole diameter
fields.startDepth: optional Num, mm the ribs start below the open end(s), default 0.5

threadRibs.notes: Only adds material, inside the hole. A hole running along the build direction is fine, unlike the roof tools.

zipTieChannel.summary: Cut a U-shaped channel under a flat face so a zip tie can loop through the part (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, the flat face each channel is cut under
fields.insetDepth: optional Num, mm below the face, default 2
fields.span: optional Num, mm between the two openings, must exceed channelHeight, default 10
fields.angle: optional Num, degrees the channel turns on the face, default 0
fields.allowBreakthrough: optional bool, default false; without it a channel reaching the part's far side is refused

elephantFootChamfer.summary: Chamfer the bottom edges of a body touching the build plate, to cancel first-layer squish (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.bodies: optional list of body ids; absent = the active body

elephantFootChamfer.notes: Finds the lowest planar face opposite the build direction and chamfers its outer edges. Edges the kernel refuses are skipped and reported rather than failing the feature; it only fails outright if none could be chamfered.

verticalFillet.summary: Fillet every edge of a body that runs parallel to the build direction (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.bodies: optional list of body ids; absent = the active body
fields.onlyConvex: optional bool, default false; true skips reflex (concave) edges

verticalFillet.notes: Edges the kernel refuses are skipped and reported rather than failing the feature; it only fails outright if none could be filleted. A reflex edge ADDS material.

fields.bodies: optional list of body ids; absent = the active body

move.notes: The rotation (X, then Y, then Z, about the WORLD origin) is applied BEFORE the translation, so to turn a part about its own centre, build it at the origin, rotate, then translate in the same move. A listed body that no longer exists is skipped with a warning. box, cylinder, cone, sphere and torus are always centred on the origin, so this (or a joint) is how they are placed.

duplicate.summary: Copy bodies and place the copies, leaving the originals in place.

fields.bodies: optional list of body ids; absent = the active body

duplicate.notes: Like move, but the source bodies stay put and each copy becomes a new body. A zero transform still makes an independent copy. The rotation is about the world origin and comes before the translation, as on move.

joint.summary: Position one body against another by aligning a mate connector on each, and re-resolve those connectors every rebuild so the assembly follows the parts.

fields.moving: body id of the body to reposition; nothing else moves
fields.mate:
MateConnector on the MOVING body, the frame brought to meet `to`. One side of a joint: a coordinate frame, an origin, a z axis that is the mating direction, and an optional x axis for rotational reference, named one of five ways:
  {"body":"body2", "face": <Selector>}   the face centre, its outward normal is the axis
  {"body":"body2", "edge": <Selector>}   the edge midpoint, its direction is the axis
  {"body":"body2", "axis": <Selector>}   a line, for pins and slides: a round face's axis through the middle of the face, a flat face's normal through its centroid, a circle's centre and normal, or a straight edge's midpoint and direction. The line points the way its largest component is positive, so a pin and the hole it sits in give the same line
  {"datum": <datumPlane id>}   follows that datum plane (a datumAxis is not supported here)
  {"origin":[x,y,z], "zdir":[x,y,z], "xdir":[x,y,z]}   an explicit world frame
A connector on geometry is a REFERENCE, re-resolved every rebuild, so the joint tracks the part as it changes. Set `body` whenever you use `face`, `edge` or `axis`. Without `xdir` the x axis is the kernel's own pick square to z, the same on both sides of a joint whose connectors give the same line.
fields.to: MateConnector on the body it mates against, held fixed
fields.mode: optional "rigid", "revolute" or "slider": which freedom the joint leaves, so the UI offers the matching handle. The placement is the same for all three.
fields.flush: optional bool. Two mating faces meet FACE TO FACE by default (their outward normals opposed); `flush` points the connector axes the same way instead, so the parts sit on the same side.
fields.offset: optional Num, mm along the mate axis (a slider's freedom)
fields.angle: optional Num, degrees about the mate axis (a revolute's freedom)

joint.notes: Body ids are body1, body2, ... handed out at build time, so read them from `build` or `inspect`. A mate reference that no longer resolves (a removed datum, a face a change deleted) leaves the moving body exactly where it is and records a diagnostic, rather than failing the build or teleporting the part.

mechanism.summary: Pose a linkage: bodies joined by revolute, slider and rigid joints, closed loops included, solved together with one joint driven to a value.

fields.ground: body id of the part that stays put; every other body a joint names is moved
fields.joints: list of joints, each {"id":"pin1", "mode":"revolute" | "slider" | "rigid", "a": MateConnector, "b": MateConnector}. `a` is on the part that moves on the joint, `b` on the part it is held by, and the joint's body on each side is the connector's `body`, else its selector's `body`. Pick pins and slides with `axis` connectors, on the pin and on its hole. A revolute keeps the two axes on one line and their offset along it as modelled; a slider keeps the parts' relative turn and their offset across the axis as modelled; a rigid joint welds the two as modelled.
fields.drive: optional id of a revolute or slider joint in `joints`, the one `angle` or `offset` moves. Without it the joints are only closed as modelled.
fields.offset: optional Num, mm. Where a slider drive goes: the offset of a's origin from b's, along b's axis.
fields.angle: optional Num, degrees. Where a revolute drive goes: the angle from b's x axis to a's, about b's axis.

mechanism.notes: Units are mm and degrees. Each connector resolves once, on the bodies as the features above left them, and then rides on its body; `ground` never moves. So copy selectors for connectors from `inspect` while the drive sits at its modelled value (or with the mechanism's `activeWhen` at 0), never from a posed build, whose faces have moved. Both drive values are measured in b's frame, so with no `xdir` on either side a's x is taken from b's and the angle reads 0 as modelled (give both sides an `xdir` to measure from a direction of your own). The solver first closes the joints from the modelled pose, then turns or slides the drive to its value in small steps, so the linkage stays on the branch it was modelled on; an angle is taken a whole number of turns from the modelled one, whichever is nearest it, so 350 and -10 give the same pose, and a rocker that cannot get there that way tries the other way round. The value that does not match the drive's mode is ignored. Bind `angle` or `offset` to a parameter to sweep the motion with `interference`. To edit one joint, resend the whole `joints` array with feature_update. A failed solve is a build error that moves nothing: "mechanism: the joints cannot all be met, pin2 stays 0.8 mm apart (body5 to body3)" when the modelled parts cannot be joined, and "mechanism: the linkage cannot reach angle 140 deg on pin1, it locks near 128.4 deg where pin2 stays 0.8 mm apart" past the end of its travel, ending at the angle when it stops at a dead point with every joint still met. A motion the joints leave free besides the drive is a warning naming the bodies that can still move. Bodies are moved, not rebuilt, so their faces keep their history.

scale.summary: Scale bodies, uniformly or per axis.

fields.factor: Num, REQUIRED even with sx/sy/sz: the uniform factor and the default for each of them. 0 is refused
fields.sx: optional Num, the factor along X; default `factor`
fields.sy: optional Num, the factor along Y; default `factor`
fields.sz: optional Num, the factor along Z; default `factor`
fields.about: optional [x,y,z] held still; default the body's placement origin, usually the world origin and NOT its centre

mirror.summary: Mirror bodies across a world plane, each fused with its reflection.

fields.plane: "XY", "XZ" or "YZ", or the id of a datumPlane above this mirror; written {"name": "YZ"} once `bodies` is set, which feature_add and feature_update do for you
fields.bodies: optional list of body ids, each fused with its own reflection; the active body when absent. A body id that does not exist at this point is an error

mirror.notes: Set `bodies` whenever more than one body exists: without it the mirror reflects the most recently CREATED body, which is rarely the one meant.

fields.operation: "union", "subtract" or "intersect" ("join" and "cut" are read as union and subtract)
fields.target: optional body id, kept and modified; default the first body
fields.tools: optional list of body ids applied to it; default every other body
fields.keepOriginals: optional bool; keeps the TOOL bodies, the target is always replaced

boolean.notes: Body ids are body1, body2, ..., NOT feature ids. Call `build` and read the body list before writing one. An intersect REPLACES the target with the overlap and fails when there is none, so it is not a clash check: use the `interference` tool for that.

fields.keep: "top" (the side the plane normal points to; on XZ that is -Y), "bottom" or "both"
fields.body: optional single body id; `bodies` wins when both are set
fields.bodies: optional list of body ids; absent = the active body. An id that does not exist is dropped

imprint.summary: Divide a face into separate faces along a sketch drawn on it, adding and removing no material.

fields.sketch: id of a sketch drawn ON the face to divide
fields.body: optional body id; default the body owning the sketch's face

imprint.notes: The curves must reach the face's edges to cut off a region; ones that don't leave the face whole and report an advisory. Each new face can then be pressed, painted or offset on its own.

datumPlane.summary: A construction plane other features can sit on.

fields.plane: PlaneSpec, the reference; with `planeId` or `face` it is only the cache used when that reference stops resolving
fields.planeId: optional id of another datumPlane feature above this one, which is preferred over `plane`: this plane then follows it
fields.face: optional Selector to follow a body face
fields.at: optional [x,y,z] pick point, needed on a round face
fields.offset: optional Num, mm along the reference normal
fields.shiftX: optional Num, mm along the reference x axis, moves the point the tilts turn about
fields.shiftY: optional Num, mm along the reference y axis
fields.tiltX: optional Num, degrees about the reference x axis through the shifted point, right handed
fields.tiltY: optional Num, degrees about the y axis as tiltX left it
fields.spin: optional Num, degrees about the normal as both tilts left it, turns the plane's own x and y
fields.name: optional label

datumPlane.notes: Placement is reference frame, then shiftX/shiftY/offset along the reference's own axes, then tiltX, tiltY and spin in that order about the resulting point. Every number is relative to the reference, so the plane follows its parent datum or face and every value can be a parameter name. A plane 20 mm above XY leaning 30 degrees: {"plane":"XY", "offset":20, "tiltX":30}.

datumPoint.summary: A reference point in space, a marker with no geometry that other features and the user can snap to.

datumAxis.summary: A reference axis, an infinite construction line a circular pattern can turn about with {"datum": "<id>"}. Revolve, mirror and joints do not read datum axes.

fields.dir: [x,y,z], its direction; need not be unit length
fields.axisEdge: optional Selector anchoring the axis to a straight model EDGE; the engine re-resolves that edge every rebuild so the axis FOLLOWS the part, and origin/dir stay as the cache it falls back to
fields.name: optional label

fields.features: optional list of feature ids, INSTEAD of bodies: repeat what those features cut or joined rather than a whole body. A hole, or an extrude, revolve, sweep or loft whose operation is cut or join, or press-pull that cut or joined, or another pattern with features. They must be above this pattern.

patternLinear.notes: Two modes. With `bodies` (or neither field) whole bodies are copied and fused, so patterning a plate with one hole gives overlapping plates. To repeat the HOLE, list the hole feature in `features`: each copy of its tool is cut from the body the hole was cut from, in one boolean, and a copy that misses the body is skipped. A fillet, chamfer, sketch, move or an extrude that made a new body cannot be patterned this way and is an error naming it. `bodies` and `features` together are an error. Copy k is moved k * spacing along the axis.

fields.angle: Num, degrees: 360 spaces `count` copies evenly around the circle; any other angle puts the first and last copies at its two ends
fields.axis: "X", "Y" or "Z" (the world axis through the origin), a line {"origin":[x,y,z], "dir":[x,y,z]} such as the vertical line through a part's centre, or {"datum": "<id>"} naming a datumAxis above this pattern (never the bare id)
fields.axisRef: optional Selector naming what the axis follows, re-resolved every rebuild: a straight edge (its line), a round edge (its centre line), a cylindrical or conical face (its axis) or a flat face (its normal through the middle of the face); is preferred over `axis`, which must then be the line {"origin", "dir"} it resolves to, the cache it falls back to
fields.features: optional list of feature ids, INSTEAD of bodies: repeat what those features cut or joined rather than a whole body. A hole, or an extrude, revolve, sweep or loft whose operation is cut or join, or press-pull that cut or joined, or another pattern with features. They must be above this pattern.

patternCircular.notes: Two modes. With `bodies` (or neither field) whole bodies are copied and fused, so patterning a plate with one hole gives overlapping plates. To repeat the HOLE, list the hole feature in `features`: each copy of its tool is cut from the body the hole was cut from, in one boolean, and a copy that misses the body is skipped. A fillet, chamfer, sketch, move or an extrude that made a new body cannot be patterned this way and is an error naming it. `bodies` and `features` together are an error. With a bare "X", "Y" or "Z" copies turn about the WORLD axis through the origin, so a bolt circle around a centred box needs no offset. A part drawn from a corner is not centred: give `axis` as a line through its centre, or `axisRef` a face or edge of it with that line as `axis`, or most copies land off the part. A build says how many copies missed the body as a warning.

fields.features: optional list of feature ids, INSTEAD of bodies: repeat what those features cut or joined rather than a whole body. A hole, or an extrude, revolve, sweep or loft whose operation is cut or join, or press-pull that cut or joined, or another pattern with features. They must be above this pattern.

patternRect.notes: Two modes. With `bodies` (or neither field) whole bodies are copied and fused, so patterning a plate with one hole gives overlapping plates. To repeat the HOLE, list the hole feature in `features`: each copy of its tool is cut from the body the hole was cut from, in one boolean, and a copy that misses the body is skipped. A fillet, chamfer, sketch, move or an extrude that made a new body cannot be patterned this way and is an error naming it. `bodies` and `features` together are an error. Without `bodies` or `features` the last body is the one copied. Copy (i, j) is moved (i * spacingX, j * spacingY, 0).

import.summary: A body read from a geometry file. Use the `doc_import` TOOL, never feature_add: `geom` is a content hash in the blob store, and only the import itself can put the geometry there, so a hand-written one names a blob that does not exist.

fields.name: label
fields.geom: content hash in the document blob store
fields.source: the file it was read from, for reference
fields.solid: Bool, false means a surface body that cannot be cut

import.notes: The tool takes `path` when the file is one this machine can open, or `content` (the file itself, base64, with `name`) when you are holding the file and your host will not give you a path to it. A text format can go as it is with encoding "text". Inline, gzip it first: STEP is text and shrinks about tenfold, which is the difference between one message and ten. Still too big? Encode the WHOLE file once, split the text that comes out, and send the pieces with `part` and `parts`, quoting the `upload` id the first reply gives back. Do not encode each piece separately, the halves of a base64 string join back up and separately encoded pieces do not. Remember that content is written by YOU: every piece is a message of your own output, so past a handful of pieces the answer is to ask for a path rather than to keep typing. An imported body is ordinary geometry once it is in: `inspect` gives its faces and edges with selectors, and it can be cut, filleted and measured against like anything else. `solid: false` means the file did not close into a watertight solid, so a boolean against it will disappoint: say so rather than press on.

organic.summary: A smooth, rounded solid from sized nodes (Node Bodies plugin): each chain of nodes becomes one limb lofted through them, a node on no chain is an ellipsoid, and everything fuses into one body.

fields.nodes: list of nodes {"id", "x", "y", "z", "sx", "sy", "sz", "rx", "ry", "rz"}: the centre in world mm, the three radii (sx default 5, sy and sz default sx) and a turn in degrees. Every value is a Num
fields.chains: optional list of chains, each a list of node ids in order, e.g. [["n1", "n2", "n3"]]
fields.blend: optional Num, mm the junctions between limbs are rounded by, default 0
fields.targets: optional list of body ids a join/cut/intersect may touch
fields.name: optional body name, default "Node body"

organic.notes: A chain that doubles back on itself tighter than its own radius folds through itself and is refused; very sharp bends pinch on the inside.

polyline.points: [[x, y], ...], each value a Num; a chain of straight lines through them, stored as `line` entities named id_1, id_2, ... (stepping round ids already used) whose shared ends are the same values, so they join. A pattern of the polyline repeats its lines; a constraint names one of the lines
polyline.closed: true to add the line from the last point back to the first, which makes it a profile (3 or more points)

arc.mx: Num, a point ON the arc between the ends

rectangle.from: optional [x, y] corner, numbers only, with `to` the opposite corner, in place of width, height, x and y; stored as the centre form

spline.points: [{x, y}, ...], the curve passes through every point

bspline.poles: [{x, y}, ...] control points: the curve is pulled toward them and passes only through the two end poles of an open curve
bspline.degree: 2, 3 or 5 (default 3), lowered to one less than the pole count when there are fewer poles
bspline.closed: true for a smooth closed loop (3 or more poles), which is a profile on its own
bspline.knots: optional, written by the app when a pole is inserted; leave it out for evenly spaced knots

sketchNotes:
Every entity may carry an `id` (unique within the sketch) and `construction: true`, which draws it without letting it bound a profile.
A profile that will be extruded or revolved must be CLOSED: consecutive endpoints must be numerically identical, not merely close.
A sketch drawn on XZ has its 2D x along world X and its 2D y along world Z.
Closed shapes that overlap are united when an extrude leaves out `regions`, holes and all. With `regions`, every overlap is an area of its own and needs its own point; `sketch_merge` replaces such shapes with the one outline around them.
howTo:
Working order that avoids most dead ends:

1. `param_set` the driving dimensions FIRST, then write features that reference
   them by name. Retrofitting parameters means rewriting every feature.
2. `feature_add` a few features, then `build`. Build often: an error names the
   feature that caused it, and one at a time is far easier to place than six.
3. `inspect` after a build to learn the body ids, the face and edge lists, and
   the ready-made selectors. Never guess a selector.
4. `view` to look at it. Numbers say a hole is 8mm across; only the picture says
   it is in the wrong place.
5. `doc_save` to a .funda file, which the app opens directly.

Asked to fit something to a part that exists as a file (STEP, STL, 3MF, OBJ,
BREP, GLB)? `doc_import` it first, then `build` and `inspect` it: that gives the
real sizes and the selectors for its faces and edges, which is what makes the
next feature something other than a guess. Import once and keep the document, a
large STEP is minutes of reading. If the file was given to you rather than left
on this machine, send it as `content` and skip looking for a path that is not
there: gzipped, and in pieces if it is still too big for one message.

If it is too big for even that, the answer is never to model against a
simplified stand-in you made up. A part fitted to an approximation of the
reference is wrong in a way nothing downstream can detect, because every
measurement you take afterwards agrees with every other one. Ask instead. The
person you are working with is at the machine FundaCAD is running on: they can
give you the file's path there, or open it themselves with File, Import Mesh,
after which it is in the document and `inspect` measures the real thing. Saying
"I cannot reach this file, what is its path on your machine?" costs one message
and gets the actual part.

Things that are true here and not in every CAD:
 - Z is up. A sketch on XY is a floor plan; a sketch on XZ is a side elevation.
 - box, cylinder and sphere are CENTRED ON THE ORIGIN. Use `move` to place them.
 - Body ids (body1, body2, ...) are handed out at build time and are NOT feature
   ids. Read them from `build` or `inspect`. A body keeps its id afterwards.
 - A feature can only reference features ABOVE it in the timeline.
